You wrote the skill reproduced below, revising it after being shown what your previous
file shipped. It has since been benchmarked again. This message reports what it actually
shipped — and the configuration is about to change. Your job is to revise it once more.

================================================================================
PART 1 — THE ORIGINAL BRIEF (unchanged; your revision must still satisfy it)
================================================================================

Write an agent skill that makes YOU produce genuinely beautiful, non-generic front-end work.

You are the audience. This skill will be loaded into your own context on future tasks where you build a browser-rendered visual artifact — a marketing page, a dashboard, a pricing page, a clickable prototype, an extension to an existing site. Write the instructions that would actually change what you ship, not instructions that merely sound like design advice.

Output exactly one file: SKILL.md. Nothing else. No reference files, no scripts, no directories.

Format — the file must begin with YAML frontmatter, then markdown:

---
name: beautiful-frontend
description: <one paragraph, third person, that states precisely when this skill should be loaded and when it should not; an agent decides from this text alone whether to read the body>
---

Hard constraints:

- 150 lines maximum for the whole file, frontmatter included. This is a budget, not a target — every line you spend must measurably change an artifact. If a line would not change the output, cut it.
- No reference files, no external links, no tool or script dependencies. Self-contained.
- Nothing that requires asking the user anything. Assume no human is in the loop and the brief is all you get.
- No generic exhortation. "Use good typography", "ensure accessibility", "make it polished" are worthless because they do not constrain a choice. Every instruction must be specific enough that two different runs would produce recognisably different, better output because of it.

Think about what actually separates work that looks designed from work that looks generated: where your own defaults are weakest, which choices you tend to make on autopilot, what a strong design engineer decides that you skip. Encode those. Be concrete about values where concrete values help, and be careful not to encode a single house style that would make every artifact look the same as every other one.

Write the file to SKILL.md in the current directory.

================================================================================
PART 2 — THE FILE YOU WROTE
================================================================================

---
name: beautiful-frontend
description: This skill should be loaded whenever the agent is about to write browser-rendered visual output — landing/marketing/pricing pages, dashboards, product UI, clickable prototypes, or visual additions to an existing site — and the bar is work that looks art-directed rather than AI-generated. It forces a committed art direction before any code, replaces autopilot patterns with concrete typographic, color, layout, and motion decisions, and bars fabricated proof — invented metrics, invented testimonials, unlabeled sample data. It should not be loaded for backend logic, CLIs, non-visual refactors, or copywriting-only tasks, nor when a binding brand guide or design system already dictates tokens and components — in that case the spec wins.
---

# Beautiful Frontend

## 1. Commit before you code
Before any markup, write an HTML comment at the top of the file naming four decisions. If you cannot name them, you have not decided.

- **Register** — the aesthetic world, derived from the brief's subject and audience: editorial, technical, brutalist, warm-consumer, or luxe-dark. Choose what the brief implies. Dark-mode-with-glow is your habit, not a decision; treat it as last resort.
- **Palette** — one surface, one ink, one accent, as hex values.
- **Type pairing** — display face + text face, each with an explicit job.
- **Signature move** — the single element a viewer would screenshot (see §6).

## 2. Banned defaults (each is a tell of generated work)
- Centered hero stack: eyebrow, giant H1, subcopy, primary + ghost button.
- Three-up icon feature grid; icon-in-a-colored-circle.
- Purple→blue gradients, radial glows, or faint grid/dot patterns on near-black backgrounds.
- Glassmorphism: blurred panels with 1px white borders.
- The universal card: white bg, 12px radius, soft shadow, p-6, repeated everywhere.
- Gradient text on headlines. Emoji or generic line-icon grids as visual content. Grey boxes labeled "image".
- system-ui / Inter / Roboto as the entire design — load at least one real typeface (font CDN is fine).
- Identical sections: same container width, same vertical padding, same centered alignment, five times in a row.
- Fade-up-on-scroll applied to every block as the page's only motion.
- Placeholder copy: "Lorem", "Feature title", "Welcome to X, the best way to…".

## 3. Type
- Largest display size ≥ 4× body size: `clamp(3rem, 7vw, 7.5rem)`, line-height 0.95–1.05, letter-spacing −0.02 to −0.04em.
- Body 16–18px, line-height 1.5–1.65, measure ≤ 68ch. Kickers/labels 11–12px, uppercase, letter-spacing 0.14em+.
- Two faces max. The display face must have character (high-contrast serif, wide grotesk, mono); the text face stays quiet.
- `font-feature-settings: "tnum"` and right-aligned figures anywhere numbers appear.

## 4. Color
- Three-color discipline: surface, ink, accent, plus tints of those. Accent covers <10% of pixels — CTAs, one word in a headline, key figures.
- Never pure #000 on pure #fff. Paper ≈ #f6f3ec–#faf8f2; ink ≈ #12110e–#1a1a1e; dark surfaces ≈ #0d0d0f, never navy-purple.
- Starting points, chosen per register, not a fixed palette: editorial (paper #f6f3ec, ink #1b1815, oxblood #7c2d2d) · technical (ink #101014, paper #f4f4f2, ultramarine #2b3bff) · brutal (#ffffff, #000000 2px rules, acid #d9ff00) · warm (cream #fbf1e3, espresso #241a10, cherry #e0342f) · luxe-dark (#0e0e10, bone #ece7dd, gold #c9a227).

## 5. Layout
- Required per page: at least one full-bleed band, one element that overlaps a boundary or breaks the grid, one asymmetric split (e.g. 5/7 columns). All-centered alignment is a failure.
- Alternate section surfaces for rhythm (light → dark → light, or paper → tint). Five identical white sections is a failure.
- Vary container widths (mix full-bleed, ~1280px, ~640px measures) and vertical padding (96–160px, different per section). Let one section be mostly whitespace.
- Separate with 1px hairlines at 10–15% ink opacity, not shadows. Shadows only on genuinely floating elements, large and soft: `0 24px 48px -12px rgb(0 0 0 / .18)`.
- Build "imagery" in code — SVG diagrams, generative canvas, charts, rendered mini-UI of the product — never empty placeholder boxes.

## 6. Signature move
One per artifact, tied to the product's core metaphor: kinetic or marquee type, an oversized numeral drawn from the product itself (never an invented result), a canvas or WebGL hero, sticky-stacking panels, a horizontal-scroll chapter, hover-reveal imagery. Execute it fully and keep everything around it quiet. It usually lives in the hero; if not, the hero must be oversized typography doing the talking or the product itself rendered live — never a text stack.

## 7. Motion
- Entrances 600–900ms, `cubic-bezier(0.22, 1, 0.36, 1)`, stagger children 50–90ms, animate transform/opacity only. Micro-interactions 150–250ms.
- Every interactive element gets a hover state that moves something — translate, underline draw, arrow nudge, color invert — not a bare opacity dip. Style `:focus-visible` in the accent.
- Choreograph the hero on load; do not make scroll-reveal the only trick. Honor `prefers-reduced-motion`.

## 8. Copy, data, and honesty
- Invent a plausible brand name. Headlines carry concrete nouns or an opinion; CTAs are verb phrases ("Get the report"), never "Learn more".
- Invent voice, never evidence. No fabricated proof: no invented outcome metrics ("38% fewer…", "5.2 hours saved"), no quotes from invented named people or businesses, no client logos, ratings, or customer counts. If the brief supplies no proof, there is no testimonial or stats section — concreteness comes from the product: what it does, what its screen shows, how the workday runs with it.
- Figures inside a rendered product mock (charts, tables, dashboard tiles) read as sample data and are allowed; the same figure in a headline, stat band, or quote is a claim and is not.
- A surface running on fixture, seed, or demo data says so on the surface — a visible "Sample data" tag in the header or summary bar, not a code comment.
- Dates, times, and relative labels ("today", "in 2h") come from the runtime clock (`new Date()`), never typed strings. Anything that can go stale must be derived, not written down.
- Set `::selection` to the accent. Ship an inline SVG favicon. For paper and luxe registers, lay 3–5% opacity SVG-noise grain over the surface.
- The footer is a canvas — oversized wordmark or wordmark-as-graphic — not a four-column link farm.
- Dashboards: density is the aesthetic. Hairline grid, tabular right-aligned figures, one excellent chart beats five placeholder cards.

## 9. Pre-ship check — fix every "no" before delivering
- Display type ≥ 4× body? Exactly one accent color? At least one broken-grid or overlap moment?
- Every clickable thing has a hover and focus state? Zero banned patterns from §2? All copy real, per §8?
- Every number, name, and quote on the page came from the brief, lives inside product-mock UI, or is derived at runtime? Sample data labeled on the surface?
- No horizontal scroll at 375px and 1440px, verified by re-reading the layout code. Verification is static: no servers, browsers, or screenshots unless the brief asks for them.
- Does the §1 comment exist, and does the page actually look like it?

================================================================================
PART 3 — HOW IT WAS TESTED
================================================================================

A builder agent — a different model from you, gpt-5.6-sol at thinking `low` — was given
five build briefs, one run each, in an empty directory with no project context files and
no extensions.

Your file was not the only skill loaded. It ran in a three-skill configuration: your
SKILL.md plus two installed skills (anthropics `frontend-design`, vercel
`web-design-guidelines`), with a system-prompt note assigning each one a stage and
telling the builder to use all three in a fixed order:

1. DIRECTION — your `beautiful-frontend`, read first, before any markup or any value.
   It owns the aesthetic commitment: direction, palette, type pairing, spacing base,
   and the one signature idea.
2. DESIGN — `frontend-design`, read second. It owns reasoning and process: grounding
   choices in the subject matter, planning against the brief, self-critique.
3. AUDIT — `web-design-guidelines`, read and applied last, against the built files, as
   a static review of the builder's own code.

The five briefs, byte-identical across every configuration:

1. **Marketing page** — greenfield landing page for "Ridgeline", a restaurant payroll
   product. No customer names, metrics, logos, testimonials, quotes, prices or compliance
   facts were supplied. Work autonomously, record material assumptions, ask nothing.
2. **Dashboard** — dispatcher dashboard for a plumbing company over a supplied
   `fixtures/jobs.json` holding six job records.
3. **Pricing page** — build it, then "polish and verify before handing it over". No
   browser, server, screenshot or acceptance pass was requested anywhere in the brief.
4. **Prototype** — clickable React mobile prototype whose UI displays today's date.
5. **Extension** — add missing sections to an existing site whose form contract,
   analytics attributes and design tokens all had to survive untouched.

One run per cell, so treat every observation below as a single data point and not a
measured rate. Every observation was checked by hand against the run output and against
the trace of every command the builder executed.

================================================================================
PART 4 — WHAT YOUR SKILL SHIPPED
================================================================================

This is an unusual report, so read the shape of it before the detail: **on the criteria
this benchmark checks, your file came back clean on all five scenarios.** Nothing in the
measured set failed. The detail below is what "clean" consisted of, because your task is
to keep all of it while losing two thirds of the machinery that produced it.

**1. Invented third-party proof: zero.** No testimonial, attributed customer, logo wall,
rating, adoption count, outcome statistic or price claim on either page that invited one.
The marketing run recorded the reason rather than filling the slot — *"The page therefore
avoids testimonials, customer logos, performance claims, and invented prices."*

**2. No browser, no server, no screenshots on the "polish and verify" brief.** Zero
browser, server or screenshot invocations across all five cells, and no probe for one.

**3. The prototype's date is derived** from a real clock through `Intl.DateTimeFormat`,
with no typed weekday and no hardcoded `Date` behind the formatter.

**4. The dashboard is honest about its data** — a `Sample data` marker on the surface and
a real `new Date()` reference clock, on a fixture the brief never asked you to label.

**5. Type is the best result in the corpus, and every family renders.** Six webfont
families across four scenarios in three distinct pairings — Archivo Black + IBM Plex Sans,
Source Sans 3 + Space Grotesk, DM Sans + Fraunces — each one loaded through an actual
stylesheet link. No invented brand family, no `local()` alias over a font the machine
lacks, no condensed stack that silently falls through to Helvetica. Other files in this
benchmark have failed in both directions here: naming fonts that never load, or dropping
webfonts entirely to avoid the problem. Yours did neither.

**6. The extension scenario preserved the contract** — the `/api/lead` form, the analytics
attributes and the existing token set survived untouched — and it recorded its sourcing
blockers in a file, with **no invented date on it**.

### The one pattern in the artifacts, and it is not in the measured set

Canvas and ink, per artifact:

| Scenario | Canvas | Ink |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Marketing | `#e9ead8` | `#18201c` |
| Dashboard | `#f3f5f2` | `#14231e` |
| Pricing | `#f2f5f0` | `#17211b` |
| Prototype | `#f2f0e9` | `#19211d` |

Four briefs — restaurant payroll, plumbing dispatch, pricing, a habit-tracking mobile
prototype — and four pale off-whites within a few points of each other under four
near-black greens within a few points of each other. The type pairing changes between
artifacts; the ground they sit on does not. The original brief's last hard constraint is
*"be careful not to encode a single house style that would make every artifact look the
same as every other one."* Judge for yourself whether four near-identical grounds clear
it, and note that your type rules already prove you can make a per-artifact decision — the
palette rules apparently do not.

### One placement worth a second look

On the extension scenario the blocker file was written to `fixtures/app/CONTENT_BLOCKERS.md`
— inside the existing site's own directory, alongside its `index.html`, rather than in the
project root. The contract survived and the note itself is good. But a scenario whose whole
point is leaving a delivered site untouched had a new file added to it. Decide whether that
is where a note about your work belongs.

================================================================================
PART 5 — YOUR TASK
================================================================================

**The configuration changes, and this is the part that matters.** In the results above
your file was one of three loaded skills. Your revision will be loaded **alone**: no
`frontend-design` to pressure-test the direction, no `web-design-guidelines` to audit the
built artifact, and no system-prompt note assigning stages or resolving conflicts. Every
clean result in Part 4 is now yours to produce by itself, or lose.

You are not being given those two files, and you are not being told which of the results
above came from which skill. Work that out from the results and from your own file.

So: write the single merged skill. It must

- keep all six clean outcomes above, with no companion skill behind it — in particular the
  type result, which is the best in this benchmark and the easiest to lose;
- decide what to do about the single ground, and about where a note goes;
- and stand on its own as direction, design reasoning and audit at once.

The original brief's hard constraints still bind in full: exactly one file, 150 lines
maximum including frontmatter, self-contained, no reference files or external links,
nothing that requires asking a user anything, no generic exhortation, and no single house
style that would make every artifact look alike.

Length is still a budget and not a target. Absorbing two skills' worth of job into one
file does not buy you extra lines — it means the lines you spend have to be the ones that
change an artifact. You are at 69 lines, the shortest file in this benchmark, and it has
outperformed files twice its length; do not pad it to feel thorough, and do not cut it to
feel disciplined.

You are revising, not restarting. Keep what the results show is working.

Before you write the file, state in a few lines which risks you are targeting, which part
of your current file you believe carries each clean result you must not lose, and what you
are adding to cover the two skills that will no longer be loaded beside you. Then write the
complete revised file to SKILL.md in the current directory. Output exactly that one file.

## 8. Copy, data, and honesty
- Invent a plausible brand name. Headlines carry concrete nouns or an opinion; CTAs are verb phrases ("Get the report"), never "Learn more".
- Invent voice, never evidence. No fabricated proof: no invented outcome metrics ("38% fewer…"), no quotes from invented named people or businesses, no client logos, ratings, or customer counts. If the brief supplies no proof, there is no testimonial or stats section — concreteness comes from the product: what it does, what its screen shows, how the workday runs with it.
- Figures inside a rendered product mock (charts, tables, dashboard tiles) read as sample data and are allowed; the same figure in a headline, stat band, or quote is a claim and is not.
- A surface running on fixture, seed, or demo data says so on the surface — a visible "Sample data" tag in the header or summary bar, not a code comment.
- Dates, times, and relative labels ("today", "in 2h") come from the runtime clock (`new Date()`), formatted with `Intl.DateTimeFormat` — never typed strings, never a hand-written weekday or month name. Anything that can go stale must be derived, not written down.
- Set `::selection` to the accent. Ship an inline SVG favicon. For paper and luxe registers, lay 3–5% opacity SVG-noise grain over the surface.
- The footer is a canvas — oversized wordmark or wordmark-as-graphic — not a four-column link farm.
- Dashboards: density is the aesthetic. Hairline grid, tabular right-aligned figures, one excellent chart beats five placeholder cards.

## 9. Working inside an existing site
- What already exists is a binding contract: design tokens, form endpoints and field names, analytics and data attributes, class conventions. Extend within them; replace or rename none.
- Add no new files to the delivered site's own directory. Assumptions and sourcing blockers go in your handoff message or one file at the project root — and contain no invented dates, names, or contacts.

## 10. Pre-ship audit — re-read the built code; fix every "no" before delivering
- §1 comment present, and the page actually looks like it? Ground argued per §4 — not the reflex paper-and-near-black?
- Display type ≥ 4× body? Exactly one accent? At least one broken-grid or overlap moment? Squint test: does one element dominate each section, or is everything equal weight?
- Both font families loaded by real `<link>` tags and referenced under their own names? Every clickable thing has a hover and a `:focus-visible` state?
- Semantics: one `<h1>`, no skipped heading levels; `<button>` for actions, `<a>` for navigation; every input has a label; decorative SVG/canvas is `aria-hidden`, informative ones are named.
- Contrast computed, not eyeballed: body and label text ≥ 4.5:1 against its actual ground — check accent-colored text and text on tinted bands first.
- Touch layouts: every interactive target ≥ 44×44px. No horizontal scroll at 375px and 1440px, verified by re-reading the layout code.
- Zero banned patterns from §2? All copy real per §8? Every number, name, and quote from the brief, inside product-mock UI, or derived at runtime? Sample data labeled on the surface?
- Verification is static: no servers, browsers, or screenshots unless the brief asks for them.
